bib.title: Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them: Overcoming Few-Shot Prompt Order Sensitivity

SOURCE: "Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them: Overcoming Few-Shot Prompt Order Sensitivity", Yao Lu, Max Bartolo, Alastair Moore, Sebastian Riedel, Pontus Stenetorp (UCL; Mishcon de Reya). ACL 2022 (Volume 1: Long Papers, pp. 8086-8098). arXiv 2104.08786.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/01-prompt-engineering/sources/lu-2022-fantastically-ordered-prompts-where-find.pdf

COVERAGE: 44,680 of 44,680 chars. I read all of it: the body, Tables 2-5, the references (skimmed), and appendix Tables 6-9 (templates, notation, dataset statistics, examples of the generated probing set). Nothing was skipped. The paper has no limitations section.

CLAIMS
- claim: With the same 4 examples, the order alone can move SST-2 accuracy from near state-of-the-art to near chance.
  number: over 85% vs around 50%
  setup: SST-2, 4-shot, all 24 orders of one fixed balanced set of 4 examples, GPT-2 0.1B-1.5B and GPT-3 2.7B-175B (Figure 1)
  quote: "some permutations have comparable performance (over 85% accuracy) to supervised training for sentiment classification, while others perform close to random (around 50%)."
  where: p.2 (8087), ~char 4,000
- claim: Bigger models reduce order sensitivity but do not remove it, and it persists on Subj for models with billions of parameters.
  number: none
  setup: Figure 1, SST-2 and Subj, 0.1B-175B
  quote: "although increasing the model size somewhat addresses it, the problem is still present for some text classification tasks (Subj in Figure 1) for models with billions of parameters."
  where: p.2
- claim: Adding examples raises accuracy but does not reduce the variance, which can even grow. Note that this was tested only up to 32 shots, on GPT-2 models (0.1B-1.5B), with at most 24 orders sampled.
  number: 1-32 shots
  setup: SST-2, GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large/XL (Figure 3)
  quote: "increasing the number of training samples leads to increases in performance. However, a high level of variance remains, even with a large number of samples and can even increase."
  where: p.3 (8088)
- claim: A good order does not transfer between models, even between sizes of the same model family.
  number: 88.7% to 51.6%; Spearman 0.05 (175B vs 2.7B)
  setup: SST-2, 24 orders of 4 examples, pairwise rank correlation across 8 model sizes (Figure 4). Off-diagonal values range from -0.35 to 0.27.
  quote: "a specific permutation's performance may drop from 88.7% to 51.6% by changing the underlying model from GPT2-XL (1.5B) to GPT2-Large (0.8B)" / "the 175B and 2.7B model only has a correlation of 0.05"
  where: p.3
- claim: Label-order patterns (e.g. NNPP vs PNPN) also fail to transfer across models.
  number: 6 label patterns
  setup: Figure 5, the same 8 models
  quote: "It is thus not possible to identify a label ordering that is performant across different models."
  where: p.3-4
- claim: Bad orders mostly fail by collapsing onto one label. Calibration (Zhao et al. 2021) raises accuracy, but the variance stays high.
  number: none (Figure 6 x-axis endpoints 51.6 and 85.2)
  setup: SST-2, GPT2-XL 1.5B, 2-shot calibrated
  quote: "the majority of failing prompts suffer from highly unbalanced predicted label distributions" / "although calibration leads to much higher performance, the variance remains high"
  where: p.4 (8089)
- claim: Method. Have the language model generate an unlabelled "probing set" from every candidate order and discard the generated labels. Score each order by entropy on that set, using GlobalE (entropy of the predicted-label histogram) or LocalE (mean per-example prediction entropy). Keep the top-4 of the 24 orders by highest entropy. No labelled dev data is needed.
  number: top k = 4 of 24
  setup: generation limited to 128 tokens, temperature 2, block n-gram repetition
  quote: "We then select top k samples ranked by highest entropy values, where k = 4 in our experiments, of the available 24 permutations as performant prompts."
  where: p.5-6 (8089-8091)
- claim: GlobalE gives an average 13% relative improvement across 11 classification tasks, and LocalE gives 9.6%. Both also lower the variance.
  number: 13%; 9.6%
  setup: GPT-2 0.1/0.3/0.8/1.5B and GPT-3 2.7B/175B; 4-shot (1-shot DBPedia, 2-shot AGNews); 5 sets × 24 orders (175B: 2 sets × 12); 256 validation examples per dataset
  quote: "GlobalE achieves, on average, a 13% relative improvement across the eleven different sentence classification tasks in comparison to prompts that do not make use of probing. LocalE provides results slightly inferior to GlobalE, with an average 9.6% relative improvement"
  where: p.7 (8091)
- claim: The gains are largest where the variance is high. For GPT-2 0.3B on SST-2, the baseline mean ± std of 61.0 ± 13.2 becomes 78.7 ± 5.2 with GlobalE, against an oracle of 85.5. For GPT-3 175B on SST-2 there is essentially no gain: 93.9 ± 0.6 against 93.9 ± 0.6. On 175B Subj, 71.2 ± 7.3 becomes 76.3 ± 3.5.
  number: up to 30% relative
  setup: Table 2 (in the extraction, the std is fused onto the mean, so "61.013.2" means 61.0 ± 13.2)
  quote: "for models that suffer from high prompt variance, our prompt selection process can show large improvements – up to 30% relative improvement. Furthermore, for tasks with low initial prompt performance variance, our method does not negatively impact performance."
  where: p.7; Table 2 p.6
- claim: On sentence-pair tasks (CB, RTE), small GPT-2 models stay near chance whatever the order. On GPT-3 175B, GlobalE improves CB by 4.9% (75.1 to 79.9).
  number: 4.9%
  setup: CB, GPT-3 175B
  quote: "prompt selection using GlobalE improves performance by 4.9% for GPT-3 175B on CB."
  where: p.7-8
- claim: Entropy probing does better than holding out half of the 4 shots as a dev set, at every GPT-2 size. On GPT-2 1.5B SST-2: split training set 71.4, GlobalE 81.8.
  number: 71.4 vs 81.8
  setup: Table 5, SST-2
  quote: "Split Training Set 62.85.3 64.26.1 75.16.8 71.47.8"
  where: p.8 (8092-8093)
- claim: The gains hold across 4 SST-2 templates. Both the order sensitivity and the improvement appear for every template.
  number: none
  setup: Tables 3-4, GPT-2 sizes
  quote: "Entropy-based probing is not sensitive to specific templates, as it consistently provides improvements for all cases."
  where: p.7
- claim: Supervised fine-tuning is far more stable across seeds than in-context learning is across orders.
  number: less than 1% std
  setup: cited from Gao et al. 2020
  quote: "different initialisations of supervised fine-tuning approaches typically result in less than 1% standard deviation for their test set performance (Gao et al., 2020)."
  where: p.2

Relevance to the target note:
- The paper does not show that orders "teach spurious patterns". Its stated mechanism is that bad orders produce skewed, degenerate predicted-label distributions.
- Its scale tests stop at 32 shots on GPT-2 (≤1.5B) and 4-shot on GPT-3 175B. It does not contradict a finding that shuffling matters little at 50-100 shots on modern models.
- Its own 175B SST-2 results already show a tiny spread (std 0.6).

LIMITS
- There is no limitations section. Concessions in the text:
  - The 175B runs use only 2 sets × 12 orders "due to the high monetary cost".
  - Evaluation uses 256-example subsamples.
  - Context-window limits force 1-2 shots on DBPedia and AGNews.
  - On CB and RTE with small models "no good prompt exists".
- Classification only, with 2022-era base models (GPT-2, GPT-3 davinci-era API). There are no instruction-tuned or chat models, and no generation or reasoning tasks.
- The shot-count analysis covers GPT-2 only and stops at 32 shots.
- The method requires enumerating n! orders, which is only practical at small n.
- Related Work claims the method beats held-out examples "(Figure 5)"; this should read Table 5.
- The paper reports the opposite conclusion to Liu et al. 2021, who found order had little effect when examples are retrieved.

BUILDS ON
- Brown et al., 2020 (GPT-3, in-context learning)
- Radford et al., 2019 (GPT-2)
- Zhao et al., 2021 ("Calibrate before use", calibration baseline and templates)
- Gao et al., 2020 (templates, fine-tuning stability, dataset setup)
- Perez et al., 2021 (true few-shot learning without a dev set)
- Liu et al., 2021 (retrieval of examples, order has little effect)
- Paulus et al., 2018 (block n-gram repetition)
- Template-design work: Shin et al., 2020; Schick and Schütze, 2020; Jiang et al., 2020

CODE: None. The method is given only as equations: GlobalE_m = Σ_v −p_v^m log p_v^m over the predicted-label frequencies on the probing set (Eq. 3), and LocalE_m = mean over the probing set of the per-example prediction entropy (Eq. 5). Probing template: "T(xi, yi) = input:xi type:yi" (p.5).

FIGURES
- Figure 1, p.1: "Four-shot performance for 24 different sample orders across different sizes of GPT-family models (GPT-2 and GPT-3) for the SST-2 and Subj datasets." Best figure candidate. A single dot-spread per model size shows the best-to-worst gap and that scale shrinks it only partly.
- Figure 4, p.3: "Training sample permutation performance correlation across different models." A near-zero correlation heatmap makes the non-transfer point at a glance.
- Figure 3, p.3: "Order sensitivity using different numbers of training samples." Variance bands from 1 to 32 shots. Useful next to the 2025 many-shot result.
- Figure 7, p.5: Probing set construction. Explains the method faster than the equations do.
- Figure 6, p.4: Label-distribution collapse, and calibration not fixing the variance.
- Figure 8, p.7: Top-K curve on GPT2-Large. A negative slope shows the ranking works.

PROBLEMS
- Table 2, 3 and 5 cells fuse the mean with the std subscript (e.g. "58.97.8" = 58.9 ± 7.8). I read them under that convention.
- Figure axis values are extracted as loose numbers. The Figure 4 and 5 matrices were readable.
- No embedded instructions were found. The extraction is otherwise clean.
